design_detail: Large collaborative replication project (meta-research; not about drugs). Sampling frame: the 488 articles in the 2008 issues of three psychology journals, Psychological Science (PSCI), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (JPSP) and Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition (JEP:LMC). Articles were offered to volunteer teams in batches; 158 became eligible during the project (November 2011 to December 2014), teams chose 111 (113 replications) and 100 replications were completed for this report (p. aac4716-2). By default the last study of each article was repeated (84 of 100), and one key result per study was named in advance and sent to the original authors. Each replication used original materials where available, had its protocol reviewed by the original authors and registered publicly, and was re-analysed by an independent analyst (pp. aac4716-1 to aac4716-2). Replication was judged by five indicators: a significant result (P < 0.05) in the original direction; the original effect inside the replication's 95% CI; a comparison of effect sizes converted to correlation coefficients (r); a fixed-effect meta-analysis of original and replication; and the replication team's own yes/no judgement. Exploratory Spearman correlations related these indicators to features of the original studies and of the replications (pp. aac4716-2 to aac4716-4).
can_establish: How often, and how strongly, 100 published findings from three prominent social and cognitive psychology journals of 2008 were reproduced when each was repeated once, with original materials and high power to detect the originally reported effects.
cannot_establish: Which individual findings are true or false (each was repeated once, and the authors conclude that no effect was established as true or as false, p. aac4716-7); the replication rate in psychology as a whole or in other fields, drug research included (p. aac4716-6); or why replications failed (the moderator analyses are exploratory correlations).

sample.recruitment: Not people but published studies: articles from the 2008 issues of PSCI, JPSP and JEP:LMC, offered to volunteer replication teams in publication order (first a pool of the first 20 articles of each journal, then 10 more at a time) and matched to teams by interest and expertise; coordinators also recruited teams with relevant experience for particular articles. 270 contributing authors (pp. aac4716-1 to aac4716-2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Of 488 articles, 158 (32%) became eligible during the project period; 111 (70%) were selected by a team, producing 113 replications (two articles had two each); 100 (88%) were completed by the deadline. Of the 47 eligible articles not claimed, 6 (13%) were judged infeasible (time, resources, instrumentation, dependence on historical events, hard-to-access samples) and 41 (87%) were eligible but not claimed, often needing specialized samples (such as macaques or people with autism), equipment (eye tracking, fMRI) or knowledge. The last experiment of each article was the default, with occasional deviations for feasibility or on the original authors' advice; the articles contained a mean of 2.99 studies (SD 1.78) (p. aac4716-2).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (studies, not people). By journal: 32 JPSP, 28 JEP:LMC and 40 PSCI replications; by subdiscipline 43 cognitive and 57 social-personality, four studies of children or infants being coded as cognitive or social. Completion by article: 39 of 64 (61%) PSCI, 31 of 55 (56%) JPSP, 28 of 39 (72%) JEP:LMC (p. aac4716-2).
sample.attrition: 13 of 113 claimed replications (12%) were not completed by the deadline because teams ran out of time or resources; they are not analysed and not compared with the completed ones (p. aac4716-2). Exclusions by indicator: 3 original null results from the significance indicator (n = 97) and from the effect-size means (n = 97); 27 from the meta-analytic means (n = 73); 25 from the meta-analytic significance (n = 75); 5 from the confidence-interval indicator (n = 95) (Table 1 note, p. aac4716-3).
sample.selection_effects: Three prominent journals from one year, social and cognitive psychology only. Teams chose which available studies to repeat, and more resource-intensive studies were less likely to be included; the authors call the sample quasi-random and say the impact of selection bias is unknown (pp. aac4716-1, aac4716-6). Only one study per article and one result per study were tested, and the chosen result was not necessarily central to the article (p. aac4716-2).

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study. The 'exposure' is replication: each original study was repeated once under a publicly registered protocol and analysis plan, with original materials where available, review of the design by the original authors and project members, a project-wide audit, and independent re-analysis of every replication from one R script (pp. aac4716-1 to aac4716-2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. Replications were planned for high power to detect the original effect sizes: average power 0.92 (median 0.95) for the 97 significant original effects (p. aac4716-4; Table 1, p. aac4716-3).

comparison.controls: Each replication is compared with its own original study (paired comparison of P values, effect sizes and confidence intervals).
comparison.matching: Original materials, procedures and key effect agreed with the original authors where possible; sample sizes differed (median df/N 54 in the originals, 68 in the replications; Table 1, p. aac4716-3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The analogue is unknown differences between original and replication in sample, setting or procedure, which the authors say could still have changed the effects observed (p. aac4716-6).

outcomes.instruments: Five indicators: (1) replication P < 0.05 in the original direction (McNemar test against the originals); (2) original effect size within the replication's 95% CI, against the expected coverage; (3) original against replication effect size as r (Wilcoxon and paired t tests, and a binomial test of the share of pairs with the larger effect in the original); (4) fixed-effect meta-analysis of each original with its replication (metafor, Fisher-z); (5) the replication team's yes/no answer to whether its results replicated the original effect. The five correlated positively with one another (r 0.22 to 0.96, median 0.57) (pp. aac4716-2 to aac4716-4).
outcomes.validity_norms: No single standard exists; the authors discuss each indicator's weaknesses: the 0.05 threshold used as a bright line, the CI method failing smaller same-direction effects and passing imprecise near-zero ones, and the meta-analysis assuming unbiased originals (pp. aac4716-4 to aac4716-5).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Reproduced' is defined separately by each of the five indicators; the 'decline' is the difference between original and replication effect sizes (r).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for the five indicators. For the exploratory moderator analyses some variables were combined into summary indicators to reduce false positives (p. aac4716-2), but Table 2 prints Spearman correlations of 13 characteristics with 5 indicators (editors' count: 65) without P values, intervals or correction (p. aac4716-3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to the quantitative indicators (registered tests, independently re-analysed). The yes/no judgement was made by each replication team about its own study.

analysis.effect_sizes: Significance: 97 of 100 original effects were positive (four with P = 0.0508, 0.0514, 0.0516 and 0.0567 counted as positive because their authors had interpreted them so); 35 of 97 replications were significant in the original direction (36.1%; 95% CI 26.6% to 46.2%), against about 89 expected from the average power of 0.92 if all original effects were true and accurately estimated (McNemar χ2(1) = 59.1, P < 0.001); mean P value 0.028 in the originals and 0.302 in the replications (p. aac4716-4). Effect sizes: mean r 0.403 (SD 0.188) in the originals against 0.197 (SD 0.257) in the replications, Wilcoxon W = 7137, P < 0.001; the original effect was larger in 82 of 99 pairs (82.8%); original and replication effects correlated (Spearman r = 0.51) (p. aac4716-5). Confidence intervals: 30 of 73 replication CIs (41.1%) contained the original effect against 78.5% expected, and 68.2% of 22 others; 47.4% overall (p. aac4716-4). Meta-analysis: 51 of 75 combined estimates (68%) excluded zero; mean combined r 0.309 (SD 0.223, n = 73) (p. aac4716-5; Table 1, p. aac4716-3). Subjective: 39 of 100 judged replicated (p. aac4716-5).
analysis.covariates: None (unadjusted paired comparisons and rank correlations).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Each replication's protocol and analysis plan were registered publicly before data collection, and the key effect was named in advance and sent to the original authors for critique (pp. aac4716-1 to aac4716-2). The project protocol was published in 2012 (ref. 24, not read). The paper does not say whether the five aggregate indicators were specified in advance, and it calls the moderator analyses exploratory (p. aac4716-2).
analysis.selective_reporting: All 100 completed replications are reported; materials, data, reports and analysis scripts are public on the Open Science Framework (pp. aac4716-1 to aac4716-2). The 13 claimed replications not completed by the deadline are not reported here (p. aac4716-2).
analysis.power: Average replication power 0.92 (median 0.95), computed against the original effect sizes (p. aac4716-4), which the paper itself argues are likely inflated by publication and reporting bias (pp. aac4716-5 to aac4716-6); power to detect the true effects was therefore lower than stated. Each effect was replicated once: the authors call the evidence broad and shallow, with little precision about individual effects (p. aac4716-6).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 100 single replications of studies from three 2008 psychology journals, 36% of results that had been significant were significant again, effects were on average about half as large, 47% of original effects fell within the replication's 95% CI and 39% were judged replicated by the teams. Rates were higher in cognitive (21 of 42) than in social psychology (14 of 55), and findings with stronger original evidence replicated more often.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and summary give these figures accurately, including the condition that the 68% combined figure assumes no bias in the original results (pp. 943, aac4716-1). The authors warn against reading the project as a verdict on single findings: a failed replication does not show that the original was a false positive, and a successful one shows reliability, not that the explanation is right (p. aac4716-6); they conclude that no effect was established as true or as false (p. aac4716-7). Two statements go further than the data: 'high-powered designs' in the abstract means power to detect the original effect sizes, which the paper argues were inflated (pp. aac4716-1, aac4716-6); and the statement that replication success was better predicted by the strength of the original evidence than by the teams' characteristics rests on exploratory rank correlations printed without P values or intervals (Table 2, p. aac4716-3). The title speaks of psychological science, while the sample is three journals, two subfields and one year, as the limitations say (p. aac4716-6).

timeline.event: Theoretical analysis cited by the project (ref. 9) as estimating that publishing and analytic practices make it likely that more than half of research results are false (p. aac4716-1)

Cited replication rates of 11% and 25% for landmark cell-biology findings from two industrial laboratories (Begley & Ellis, 2012; Prinz et al., 2011), described by the authors as hard to interpret for want of details (p. aac4716-1); not read
Many Labs replication project (Klein et al., 2014), cited as the complementary narrow-and-deep approach of many replications of single effects (p. aac4716-6); not read
This report: 35 of 97 significant findings significant again on one replication; mean effect size halved

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no later replication project, and neither of the two related items that Science lists with the article in vol. 351, issue 6277, p. 1037 (the journal's information page, PDF p. 10), was read for this card. Within the paper, the result is a single broad-and-shallow estimate for three journals in 2008, which the authors present as an initial estimate, pointing to narrow-and-deep projects and an effort in cancer biology as complements (p. aac4716-6).

funding.funder: Center for Open Science and the Laura and John Arnold Foundation (Acknowledgments, p. aac4716-8).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no financial conflict of interest with the reported research (p. aac4716-8).
funding.affiliations_note: The corresponding author and several co-authors list the Center for Open Science, one of the two funders, as an affiliation (p. aac4716-8). The authors are psychologists examining their own discipline, which they give as the reason for studying psychology (p. aac4716-6); they are listed alphabetically. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated, multi-site replications of a random sample of published findings (not only those feasible at low cost), with protocols agreed with the original authors and power calculated against conservative effect sizes, in several fields including drug research; and, for any single finding, several independent high-powered replications.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Articles of 2008 in three prominent journals, social and cognitive psychology only: appropriate for those journals, not for psychology as a whole or for other fields, as the authors say (p. aac4716-6).

Quasi-random: articles were offered in publication order, but teams chose which to repeat; 47 of 158 eligible articles were not claimed, often for needing special samples or equipment, and resource-intensive studies were less likely to be included (pp. aac4716-2, aac4716-6).

100 replications estimate the overall significance rate within about ±10 percentage points (95% CI 26.6% to 46.2%, p. aac4716-4); journal-by-field rates rest on 15 to 31 studies, and each effect was replicated only once.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Journals, subdisciplines, sample sizes, power and effect sizes are reported (Table 1, p. aac4716-3), with study-level data and reports on the Open Science Framework (pp. aac4716-1 to aac4716-2).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 100 completed replications enter the significance and subjective indicators, but the confidence-interval and meta-analytic indicators cover only 95, 75 and 73 study pairs (Table 1 note, p. aac4716-3).

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Five complementary indicators of replication, each with its weaknesses stated (pp. aac4716-2 to aac4716-5); no single indicator is relied on.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Common protocol, registered analysis plans, project-wide audit and independent re-analysis of every replication from one R script (p. aac4716-2).

Paired tests suit the main comparisons; the fixed-effect meta-analysis assumes unbiased originals, as the authors state (p. aac4716-5); the moderator correlations in Table 2 have no P values, intervals or multiplicity control, and several are true by construction (reporting issues).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Read as completion: 100 of 113 claimed replications (88%) were completed; the reasons for non-completion (time, resources) are given, but completed and uncompleted replications are not compared (p. aac4716-2).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI items applied to a sample of published studies, as the round brief asks for studies of how research is reported. The replications were done to a high standard (registered protocols, original materials, review by the original authors, independent re-analysis), so the main figures are sound for what they measure; the limits come from the sample (three journals, two subfields, one year, teams choosing feasible studies) and from single replication attempts. The source may be cited for how often, in this sample, published significant findings were significant again on one repetition (35 of 97), for the halving of average effect sizes, for the other four replication rates, for the gap between cognitive and social psychology, for the higher replication of findings with stronger original evidence, and for its authors' statement that a single study almost never settles a question. It may not be cited as the proportion of false findings in psychology or in drug research, nor as showing that any particular finding is false.

key_findings.finding: Of 97 original results that were statistically significant (or treated as such), 35 (36.1%; 95% CI 26.6% to 46.2%) were significant again in the same direction when replicated, against about 89 expected from the replications' average power (0.92) if all original effects had been true and accurately estimated (McNemar χ2(1) = 59.1, P < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Evaluating replication effect against null hypothesis of no effect, 1st paragraph (p. aac4716-4); Table 1, Overall row (p. aac4716-3)

key_findings.finding: Four original results with P = 0.0508, 0.0514, 0.0516 and 0.0567 had been interpreted as positive by their authors and were counted as significant.
key_findings.locator: Method › Statistical analyses › Significance and P values (p. aac4716-2); Results › Evaluating replication effect against null hypothesis of no effect, 1st paragraph (p. aac4716-4)

key_findings.finding: Mean P value 0.028 in the original studies and 0.302 in the replications. The authors call treating 0.05 as a bright line between success and failure a key weakness of the significance criterion; the 64 non-significant replication P values were widely spread and deviated only slightly from the uniform distribution expected with no effect (χ2(128) = 155.83, P = 0.048), which they read as at least one possible false negative but not low power as the only explanation for failures.
key_findings.locator: Results › Evaluating replication effect against null hypothesis of no effect, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 1A

key_findings.finding: Replication effect sizes were on average half the original ones: mean r 0.403 (SD 0.188) against 0.197 (SD 0.257) (Wilcoxon W = 7137, P < 0.001); the original effect was the larger in 82 of 99 pairs (82.8%); original and replication effect sizes correlated (Spearman r = 0.51, P < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparing original and replication effect sizes, 1st paragraph (starts p. aac4716-4, numbers on p. aac4716-5); Fig. 1B; Fig. 3 (p. aac4716-6)

key_findings.finding: The original effect size lay within the replication's 95% CI for 30 of 73 study pairs with computable standard errors (41.1%, against 78.5% expected) and for 68.2% of 22 pairs tested with other statistics; 47.4% in all (Table 1: 47%, n = 95).
key_findings.locator: Results › Evaluating replication effect against original effect size, 1st paragraph (p. aac4716-4); Table 1 (p. aac4716-3)

key_findings.finding: Combining each original with its replication in a fixed-effect meta-analysis, 51 of 75 effects (68%) had 95% CIs excluding zero (mean combined r 0.309, SD 0.223, n = 73). The authors add that if publication, selection and reporting biases completely explain the differences, the replication estimates would be better estimates than the meta-analytic and original ones, but that to the extent other influences (sample, setting, quality of replication) operate, the relative bias is unknown. [The card left out 'completely' and the counter-condition.]
key_findings.locator: Results › Combining original and replication effect sizes for cumulative evidence, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. aac4716-5); Table 1 (p. aac4716-3)

key_findings.finding: Replication teams judged 39 of 100 replications successful, close to the significance results.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective assessment of 'Did it replicate?', 1st paragraph (p. aac4716-5); Table 1 (p. aac4716-3)

key_findings.finding: By the significance criterion, 21 of 42 cognitive psychology effects (50%) replicated against 14 of 55 social psychology effects (25%); by journal and field from 7 of 31 (23%, JPSP social) to 8 of 15 (53%, PSCI cognitive). Mean effect size fell from r 0.29 to 0.07 in JPSP social, 0.47 to 0.27 in JEP:LMC cognitive, 0.39 to 0.21 in PSCI social and 0.53 to 0.29 in PSCI cognitive; the declines were similar across journals and fields (χ2(3) = 2.45, P = 0.48).
key_findings.locator: Results › Correlates of reproducibility, 1st paragraph (p. aac4716-5); Table 1 (p. aac4716-3)

key_findings.finding: Among significant original effects, 23 of 49 main or simple effects (47%) replicated at P < 0.05 against 8 of 37 interaction effects (22%).

Findings with stronger original evidence replicated more often: 26 of 63 (41%) with original P < 0.02, 6 of 23 (26%) with P between 0.02 and 0.04, and 2 of 11 (18%) with P > 0.04; 20 of 32 (63%) with original P < 0.001. Spearman correlations with a significant replication: original P value −0.327, original effect size 0.304, surprising original result −0.244, replication power 0.368, experience and expertise of the original team −0.072 and of the replication team −0.096.
key_findings.locator: Results › Correlates of reproducibility, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. aac4716-5); Table 2 (p. aac4716-3)
key_findings.note: The three P-value groups add up to 34 significant replications, not the 35 of Table 1 (reporting issues). Table 2 gives no P values or intervals.

key_findings.finding: The authors attribute the smaller replication effects plausibly to publication, selection and reporting biases in the originals (low-powered designs combined with publication bias favouring positive results), the replications being confirmatory and fully reported, while allowing that differences in sample, setting or quality of replication could also contribute.
key_findings.locator: Results › Combining original and replication effect sizes for cumulative evidence, 2nd paragraph (p. aac4716-5); Discussion › Insights on reproducibility, 3rd paragraph (p. aac4716-6)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that a failure to replicate does not show that the original was a false positive (a replication can differ in ways that hide an effect), and that a successful replication mainly shows that a result is reliable, not that its explanation is correct.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Insights on reproducibility, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In their conclusion the authors say that the project established no effect as true and none as false, and that “a single study almost never provides definitive resolution for or against an effect”.

Stated limitations: unknown generalization to the rest of psychology or to other disciplines; one study per article and one result per study replicated; resource-intensive studies less likely to be included; impact of selection bias unknown; single replication attempts give little precision about individual effects.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Implications and limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The breakdown by original P value gives 26 of 63, 6 of 23 and 2 of 11 significant replications, which add up to 34, while Table 1 and the Results give 35 of 97; the denominators add up to 97.
reporting_issues.consequence: One significant replication is unaccounted for in the breakdown; the rates per group (41%, 26%, 18%) may each be off by one study. The overall 35 of 97 is stated consistently elsewhere.

reporting_issues.issue: Two counts are given for the pool of articles: one hundred fifty-eight eligible articles (64 PSCI, 55 JPSP, 39 JEP:LMC), and articles made available for selection numbering 68 PSCI, 59 JPSP and 40 JEP:LMC (editors' sum: 167); the difference of 9 is not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; it does not change the replication results, but the size of the frame from which studies were chosen is not stated consistently.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints Spearman correlations of 13 study characteristics with 5 indicators (editors' count: 65) without P values, intervals or correction for multiple testing, and some rows correlate an indicator with the quantity it is built from (replication P value with a significant replication, −0.828; original and replication effect sizes with the meta-analytic estimate, 0.793 and 0.850).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which moderators matter cannot be judged from the table, and the largest correlations are true by construction rather than findings.

reporting_issues.issue: The journal's editor's summary appended to the PDF describes the 100 studies as experiments, while the article describes experimental and correlational studies.
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 10 (journal information page); p. aac4716-1
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the article's own description of the sample.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, Science 349(6251), aac4716; journal download of 10 June 2018), all 10 PDF pages: the Research Article Summary printed p. 943 (PDF p. 1), the article printed pp. aac4716-1 to aac4716-8 (PDF pp. 2–9; anchors cite these printed labels) and the journal's unnumbered information page with the editor's summary (PDF p. 10). Tables 1 and 2 and Figures 1–3 checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, Table 1 also at 300 dpi; figure values not extracted. The supplementary materials (Materials and Methods, Figs S1–S7, Tables S1–S4) and the Open Science Framework files were not among the files and were not read.
